questions.stem: Which part of a plant makes the seeds?
options: The stem that holds the plant up

explain.why: The stem supports the plant and carries water. It does not make seeds.
The root takes in water and mineral salts. It does not make seeds.
The leaf makes food. It does not make seeds.

solution: The flower is the part that makes the seeds.

figure.alt: A potted plant in line art.

questions.stem: What is one job of the fruit of a plant?
options: To protect the seeds as they grow inside it
To take in water for the plant
To hold the plant up in the wind
To make food for the plant

explain.why: Water is taken in by the roots, not by the fruit.
Holding the plant up is the job of the stem and roots.
Food is made by the leaves, not by the fruit.

solution: The fruit covers and protects the seeds while they grow.

figure.alt: A fruit cut open, showing its skin, the soft part and a large seed inside.

questions.stem: Why do many flowers have bright petals?
options: To make food for the plant
To attract insects to the flower
To take in water for the plant from the soil

explain.why: Food is made by the leaves, not the petals.
Holding the plant up is done by the stem, not by the petals.
Water is taken in by the roots, not by petals.

solution: Bright petals attract insects that visit the flower.

figure.alt: A flower cut in half, showing its petals and the parts inside.

questions.stem: What is the job of a seed?
options: To make food for the plant
To grow into a new plant
To take in water for the plant

explain.why: Food is made by the leaves, not by a seed.
Holding the leaves up is the job of the stem.
Taking in water is the job of the roots.

solution: A seed can grow into a new plant when it gets what it needs.

figure.alt: A bean seed cut open, showing its outer covering and the parts inside.

questions.stem: A farmer picks guavas from a tree. Which part of the plant is a guava?

explain.why: Seeds are found inside the guava. The whole guava is the fruit.
Roots grow in the soil. A guava grows on the tree.
A guava starts as a flower, but the part we pick is the fruit.

solution: A guava is a fruit, with seeds inside.

questions.stem: Look at the picture of the flower cut in half. Which part is brightly coloured and attracts insects?

explain.why: Part D is at the base of the flower and later grows into the fruit.
Part C is inside the flower. It receives pollen and is not the bright outer part.
Part B is inside the flower and makes pollen. It is not there to attract insects.

solution: Part A is a petal. Bright petals attract insects.

figure.alt: A flower cut in half in line art, showing its petals and the parts inside, with four marked positions.

questions.stem: Look at the picture of the bean seed cut open. Part A covers the outside of the seed. What is the job of part A?
options: To take in water and mineral salts for the young plant
To protect the parts inside the seed
To make food for the seed
To attract insects to the seed

explain.why: Water is taken in by the root of the young plant, not by the covering.
Seeds do not make food. Leaves make food once the plant grows.
Insects are attracted to the flower, not to the seed covering.

solution: The outer covering of a seed protects the parts inside.

figure.alt: A bean seed cut open in line art, showing its outer covering and the parts inside, with three marked positions.

questions.stem: The soft part of the mango (part A) is eaten by animals, which may drop the seed (part B) far away. How does this help the mango tree?
options: More leaves grow on the tree
The seeds are spread to new places far away
The flowers open earlier in the year
The roots take in more water

explain.why: Eating the fruit does not make more leaves grow.
Animals eating the fruit do not make flowers open earlier.
Eating the fruit does not change how much water the roots take in.

solution: Animals that eat the fruit spread the seeds to other places.

figure.alt: A mango cut open in line art, showing its skin, the soft part and a large seed inside, with three marked positions.

questions.stem: In the picture of the flower cut in half, which part grows into the fruit after the flower has been pollinated?

explain.why: Part A is a petal. Petals attract insects and later fall off.
Part B makes pollen. It does not grow into the fruit.
Part C receives the pollen. It does not grow into the fruit.

solution: Part D is at the base of the flower. After pollination it grows into the fruit.

figure.alt: A flower cut in half in line art, showing its petals and the parts inside, with four marked positions.

questions.stem: Sara picks all the flowers from a chilli plant. What will the plant not be able to make?

explain.why: New stems grow from the stem tips and do not need flowers.
New roots grow from the roots already there. They do not need flowers.
New leaves grow from the stem. They do not need flowers.

solution: Fruits and seeds form from flowers, so without flowers no fruits form.

questions.stem: A bean seed has its food store (part B) removed and is then planted. What is most likely to happen?
options: The young plant gets food from its seed coat instead
The young plant grows faster because it has less to carry
The young plant grows poorly with less food
The young plant makes seeds sooner

explain.why: The seed coat protects the seed and does not provide food.
The food store feeds the young plant, so it grows poorly without it.
A young plant with less food would not make seeds sooner.

solution: The food store feeds the young plant until its leaves can make food.
Without it, the young plant has far less food.

figure.alt: A bean seed cut open in line art, showing its outer covering and the parts inside, with three marked positions.

questions.stem: Which row about the flower, fruit and seed is correct?
options: Flower: makes food; fruit: grows into a plant; seed: makes seeds
Flower: grows into a plant; fruit: makes seeds; seed: protects the fruit
Flower: protects seeds; fruit: makes seeds; seed: makes food
Flower: makes seeds; fruit: protects them; seed: grows into a plant

explain.why: Leaves make food, and a fruit does not grow into a plant. A seed does.
Seeds grow into plants and do not protect the fruit.
Flowers make seeds and fruits protect them. Seeds do not make food.

solution: The flower makes the seeds.
The fruit protects the seeds.
A seed can grow into a new plant.

questions.stem: What is the movement of pollen from one flower to another called?

explain.why: Fertilisation is when a male and a female cell join. It happens after pollination.
Germination is when a seed starts to grow into a young plant.
Seed dispersal is the spreading of seeds away from the parent plant.

solution: Moving pollen from one flower to another is called pollination.

figure.alt: A flower cut in half, showing its petals and the parts inside.

questions.stem: Which of these animals often carry pollen from flower to flower?

explain.why: Worms and snails stay low on the ground and do not visit flowers to feed.
These stay mostly on the ground or in the soil.
Fish and frogs live in or near water, not among flowers.

solution: Bees and butterflies visit flowers for the sweet nectar, so pollen sticks to them and is carried on.

figure.alt: A flower cut in half, showing its petals and the parts inside.

questions.stem: Which of these things must a bean seed have to start growing?

explain.why: These are not needed for a seed to germinate.
A seed does not need light, soil or wind to start growing.
A seed needs none of these to begin to grow.

solution: A seed needs water, air and warmth to germinate.

figure.alt: A bean seed cut open, showing its outer covering and the parts inside.

questions.stem: What do we call it when a seed starts to grow into a young plant?

explain.why: Seed dispersal is the spreading of seeds.
Fertilisation is the joining of a male and a female cell inside the flower.
Pollination is the movement of pollen between flowers.

solution: A seed starting to grow is germination.

figure.alt: A bean seed cut open, showing its outer covering and the parts inside.

questions.stem: In the picture of the bean seed cut open, part C is the tiny young plant inside. What will part C grow into?
options: The fruit that holds the seeds
The food store of the seed

explain.why: The covering is part A and does not grow into the new plant.
A fruit forms from the flower, not from the young plant inside the seed.
The food store is a different part (part B).

solution: Part C is the young plant, or baby plant, inside the seed.
It grows into a new plant.

figure.alt: A bean seed cut open in line art, showing its outer covering and the parts inside, with three marked positions.

questions.stem: What do we call the carrying of seeds away from the parent plant?

explain.why: Fertilisation is the joining of a male and a female cell.
Pollination is the movement of pollen.
Germination is when a seed starts to grow.

solution: Carrying seeds away from the parent plant is called seed dispersal.

questions.stem: Why is it good for a plant to have its seeds carried far away from it?
options: The seeds can make food for the parent plant
The parent plant can make more flowers
The seeds can grow into fruits right away
The young plants have more room and light

explain.why: Seeds do not make food for the parent plant.
Where seeds land does not change how many flowers the parent makes.
Seeds do not become fruits. They grow into new plants.

solution: Seeds that fall next to the parent must share its light, water and space.
Seeds carried far away have more room to grow.

questions.stem: Which of these seeds is carried away by the wind?

explain.why: A mango is a juicy fruit. Animals eat it and spread the seed.
A burr has hooks, so it is carried on animals' fur.
A coconut is spread by water, not wind.

solution: A dandelion seed has light hairs that catch the wind and carry it away.

questions.stem: Which of these seeds is carried away by water?
options: A seed in a bright red berry
A seed with a light wing

explain.why: A hooked seed is carried on animals' fur.
A bright berry is eaten by animals, which spread the seed.
A winged seed is carried by wind.

solution: A coconut has a thick husk that floats, so water can carry it away.

questions.stem: Birds eat red berries and later drop the seeds in their droppings far away. How are the seeds spread?

explain.why: The seeds are carried inside the bird, not blown by wind.
The fruit is eaten. It does not split open to throw the seeds out.
Water does not carry the seeds in this case.

solution: Animals eat the fruit and drop the seeds somewhere else, so the seeds are spread by animals.

questions.stem: The ripe fruits of a rubber tree dry in the sun and burst with a snap. The seeds land far from the tree. How are the seeds spread?

explain.why: No animal is needed. The fruit bursts open by itself.
The fruits dry in the sun. Water is not involved.
Wind does not throw the seeds. The fruit bursts by itself.

solution: Some fruits dry and burst open, which throws the seeds away from the plant.

questions.stem: Which of these plants makes spores instead of seeds?

explain.why: A bean plant makes flowers, pods and seeds.
A hibiscus makes flowers and seeds.
A mango tree makes flowers, fruits and seeds.

solution: Ferns do not make flowers or seeds.
They make tiny spores.

questions.stem: A gardener pushes a cut branch of a rose bush into wet soil. Weeks later it has roots and leaves and is a new rose plant. What did the new plant grow from?
options: A part of the old plant
A seed hidden inside the branch
A fruit of the old plant

explain.why: No seed was planted. The branch itself grew roots and leaves.
Pollen does not grow into a plant by itself.
A fruit was not planted, only the cut branch.

solution: A new plant can grow from a cut piece of stem.
No seed was planted.

questions.stem: Pollen is made in the male part of a flower called the ____.

explain.why: The stalk holds up the flower. It does not make pollen.
The ovary is the female part. It holds the tiny egg cells that become seeds.
Petals attract insects. They do not make pollen.

solution: The stamen is the male part of the flower and makes pollen.

figure.alt: A flower cut in half, showing its petals and the parts inside.

questions.stem: After a flower has been pollinated and fertilised, which part of it grows into the fruit?

explain.why: The stalk holds up the flower and does not become the fruit.
The petals usually wither and fall off.
The stamen makes pollen. It does not become the fruit.

solution: The ovary holds the tiny egg cells.
After fertilisation, it grows into the fruit and the egg cells become seeds.

questions.stem: A bean seed is planted in soil. Where does the young plant get its food before its leaves can make food?
options: From the food stored in the seed

explain.why: Sunlight is only used by leaves to make food, and there are no leaves yet.
Soil gives water and mineral salts, but not food.
Air alone cannot feed a young plant that has no leaves yet.

solution: A bean seed has a food store inside it.
The young plant uses this until its leaves can make food.

figure.alt: A bean seed cut open, showing its outer covering and the parts inside.

questions.stem: Which of these must happen first before a flower can make seeds?
options: The seeds are spread by wind

explain.why: Growing from a seed happens after the seed has been made.
Seeds are spread only after they have been made.
The fruit forms only after pollination, so this comes later.

solution: Seeds can form only after pollen reaches the female part of a flower.
Spreading and growing of seeds come later.

figure.alt: A flower cut in half, showing its petals and the parts inside.

questions.stem: A bean seed is put on dry cotton wool in a warm room. After a week it has not started to grow. What is missing?

explain.why: Wind is not needed for a seed to start to grow.
A seed can start to grow without soil, for example on wet cotton wool.
A seed does not need light to start to grow.

solution: A seed needs water, air and warmth to germinate.
The room is warm and has air. The cotton wool is dry, so water is missing.

figure.alt: A bean seed cut open, showing its outer covering and the parts inside.

questions.stem: The picture shows a flower cut in half. Which part makes pollen?

explain.why: Part D is the ovary, which holds the ovules. It does not make pollen.
Part C is the stigma, which receives pollen. It does not make it.
Part A is a petal. Petals are brightly coloured to attract insects. They do not make pollen.

solution: Pollen is made in the anther (part B).

questions.stem: In the picture of the flower, pollen from another flower must land on which part for the flower to make seeds?

explain.why: Part S is an anther. It makes pollen and has pollen on it already.
Part Q is the ovary. Pollen lands on the stigma at the top, not on the ovary.
Part R is a petal. Insects may land on it, but the pollen must reach the stigma.

solution: Pollen has to land on the stigma (part P). That is called pollination.

questions.stem: The picture shows a flower cut in half. After fertilisation, which part will grow into a seed?

explain.why: Part A is the stigma. It only receives pollen and does not become the seed.
Part D is an anther. It makes pollen and does not become the seed.
Part C is a petal. Petals wither after pollination.

solution: Part B is the ovule inside the ovary. After fertilisation, the ovule grows into the seed.

questions.stem: The picture shows a flower cut in half. After pollination and fertilisation, which part grows into the fruit?

explain.why: Part Y is the stigma. It receives pollen and does not grow into the fruit.
Part W is an anther. It makes pollen, and it dries up after the pollen is gone.
Part Z is a petal. Petals wither after pollination.

solution: The ovary (part X) holds the ovules. It grows into the fruit and the ovules become seeds.

questions.stem: Look at the picture of the flower. Part D is a thin stalk that holds up part C. What is the job of part D?
options: To grow into the fruit once pollination has taken place
To catch pollen that is brought from other flowers
To hold the anther up where pollen can be carried off
To make the pollen that the flower needs for seeds

explain.why: The ovary (part A) grows into the fruit, not the stalk.
Pollen is caught by the stigma (part B).
Pollen is made in the anther (part C), not in the stalk that holds it.

solution: Part D is the filament. It holds the anther up where wind or insects can reach the pollen.

questions.stem: A flower has small green petals and no smell. Its anthers hang outside the flower and its stigma is feathery. How is this flower most likely pollinated?

explain.why: Butterflies visit bright, sweet-smelling flowers, which this flower is not.
Bees are attracted by large, bright, scented flowers with nectar. This flower has none of these.
Birds that pollinate flowers visit large, brightly coloured flowers.

solution: Small dull flowers with hanging anthers and a feathery stigma are made for wind pollination.

questions.stem: Which of these features helps a flower to be pollinated by insects?
options: It makes a sweet liquid in the flower
Its petals are small and green
Its pollen is very light and dry
Its stigma hangs far outside the flower

explain.why: Small green petals do not attract insects. They belong to wind-pollinated flowers.
Very light, dry pollen is blown by the wind. Insect flowers have sticky pollen.
A stigma that hangs out is found on wind-pollinated flowers, to catch pollen from the air.

solution: The sweet liquid (nectar) makes insects come to the flower, and pollen sticks to them as they feed.

questions.stem: Grass flowers are pollinated by the wind. Why does a grass flower make a very large amount of pollen?
options: The pollen turns into the fruit
Most pollen is blown away and little lands on a stigma
The pollen is needed to make the petals bright
The pollen must feed the insects that visit the flower

explain.why: The fruit grows from the ovary, not from the pollen.
Pollen has nothing to do with the colour of the petals.
Grass flowers are not visited by insects for food. The wind carries the pollen.

solution: The wind blows pollen in all directions, so a lot is wasted.
Making a lot gives a better chance that some lands on a stigma.

questions.stem: A bee visits a flower P and then a flower Q of the same kind. Where must some pollen from flower P land for a seed to form in flower Q?
options: On the stigma of flower Q
On a petal of flower Q, which attracts the bee
On the stem that holds up flower Q
On the anther of flower Q, which makes pollen

explain.why: A petal only attracts insects. Pollen on a petal cannot lead to seeds.
Pollen on the stem cannot reach the ovules.
The anther makes pollen. Pollen must land on a stigma.

solution: Pollination is when pollen lands on a stigma of a flower of the same kind.

questions.stem: A farmer covers some flowers of a gourd plant with net bags that keep insects out. These flowers do not make fruits. What is the best reason?
options: The anthers made too much pollen
The petals did not get enough sunlight
The roots could not take in water
Pollen was not carried to the stigmas

explain.why: Too much pollen would not stop a fruit forming. The stigma needs to receive pollen.
The net bags let light in, and petals do not make the fruit.
The bags cover the flowers, not the roots.

solution: Insects carry pollen from flower to flower.
Without insects, no pollen reaches the stigmas, so no seeds or fruits form.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes fertilisation in a flowering plant?
options: An insect carries pollen from one flower to another
Pollen from an anther lands on a stigma
A male cell from pollen joins a female cell in an ovule
A seed is carried far away from the parent plant

explain.why: That is how pollen is carried. It is not fertilisation.
That is pollination. Fertilisation happens afterwards, when the cells join.
That is seed dispersal, which happens after the seed has formed.

solution: In fertilisation, a male cell from the pollen joins a female cell inside an ovule.

questions.stem: Kai put bean seeds on cotton wool in dishes P, Q, R and S as shown in the table. In which dish will the seeds most likely germinate?

explain.why: S is dry and cold, so it lacks both water and warmth.
The cotton wool in P is dry. Seeds need water to germinate.
R is inside a fridge. Seeds need warmth to germinate.

solution: Seeds need water, air and warmth to germinate.
Only Q has wet cotton wool in a warm room.

explain.why: At 15 °C only 4 seeds germinated, fewer than at 25 °C.
At 45 °C no seeds germinated. This is too hot.
At 5 °C no seeds germinated. This is too cold.

solution: The highest point on the graph is at 25 °C, with 9 seeds germinated.

explain.why: R has hooks, which catch on an animal's fur. The animal does not need to eat it.
S is light and hollow, so it floats on water.
P has a thin wing, so the wind carries it away.

solution: A soft, sweet, bright fruit is eaten by animals. The seeds pass out in the droppings far from the parent plant.

explain.why: S is light and waterproof and floats on water.
Q is soft and sweet and is spread by animals that eat it.
P has a wing, so it is carried by the wind.

solution: The small hooks of R catch on fur and clothes, so the fruit is carried to new places.

explain.why: Q is a juicy fruit that animals eat.
P is dry and light with a wing. It is made for the wind.
R has hooks and sticks to animals.

questions.stem: Tiny brown dots form on the underside of a fern leaf. Each dot holds many spores. Which statement about the spores is correct?
options: The spores stay on the leaf and grow into new ferns there
The spores must be carried by bees from fern to fern
The spores are the fruits that grow on the fern leaf
The spores are blown away and may grow into new ferns in damp places

explain.why: Spores are blown away from the parent fern. They do not grow on the leaf.
Spores are carried by the wind. Ferns have no flowers to attract bees.
Ferns do not make flowers or fruits. Spores are not fruits.

solution: Ferns reproduce by spores. The very light spores are blown by the wind.
A spore that lands in a damp place can grow into a new fern.

questions.stem: Small plantlets grow along the edge of a leaf of a Bryophyllum plant. When they fall onto soil, they grow into new plants. From which part of the parent plant do the new plants grow?

explain.why: No flower is needed. The plantlets grow on the leaf.
The plantlets are on the leaf edge, not on the roots.
These new plants do not come from seeds.

solution: The new plants grow from the leaf of the parent plant, without seeds.

questions.stem: A strawberry plant sends out long stems along the ground. A new plant grows at the end of each stem. Which statement about this is correct?
options: The new plants grow only when the parent dies
The new plants grow from spores on the stems
The new plants grow only after bees pollinate the stems
The new plants grow without seeds

explain.why: The parent plant keeps living while the new plants grow.
Strawberry plants are flowering plants. They do not make spores.
Pollination is about flowers making seeds. These stems are not flowers.

solution: The long stems grow new plants. No seeds are needed for this way of reproducing.

questions.stem: A gardener wants new plants without waiting for any flower to be pollinated first. Which of these should he plant?

explain.why: A mango seed also comes from a pollinated flower.
A seed forms only after a flower has been pollinated and fertilised.
A sunflower seed also forms after pollination.

solution: Seeds only form after pollination and fertilisation.
A piece of rose stem can grow roots and leaves into a new plant with no flowers involved.

questions.stem: The picture shows a flower cut in half. The ovary of this flower holds 3 ovules. All 3 ovules are fertilised. How many seeds can the fruit have?

explain.why: One ovule makes one seed. The number of seeds cannot be more than the number of ovules.
All 3 ovules are fertilised, so 3 seeds form, not 2.
Each fertilised ovule becomes one seed, so 3 ovules give more than 1 seed.

solution: Each fertilised ovule grows into one seed.
3 fertilised ovules give 3 seeds.

questions.stem: A tomato fruit has 40 seeds. How many ovules in the flower were fertilised to form this fruit?

explain.why: Each seed comes from one fertilised ovule, so there must be as many ovules as seeds.
A flower's ovary has many ovules. Each seed comes from its own ovule.
Each ovule makes one seed, not two.

solution: One fertilised ovule makes one seed, so 40 seeds come from 40 fertilised ovules.

questions.stem: Which of the following lists the events in the correct order, from first to last?
options: Fertilisation, pollination, fruit and seeds form, seeds are dispersed
Pollination, seeds are dispersed, fertilisation, fruit and seeds form
Pollination, fruit and seeds form, fertilisation, seeds are dispersed
Pollination, fertilisation, seeds form, seeds are dispersed

explain.why: Pollen must land on the stigma before the cells can join, so pollination comes first.
Seeds are dispersed only after they have formed.
The fruit and seeds form only after fertilisation.

solution: Pollen lands on the stigma, then the cells join, then the ovary and ovules grow, and the seeds are carried away.

questions.stem:
Which of the following statements about pollination are correct?
A: Pollen lands on the stigma.
B: Pollen can only be carried by insects.
C: Pollination happens before fertilisation.
D: Pollination is when a male cell joins a female cell.

explain.why: D is wrong. The joining of the male and female cells is fertilisation, not pollination.
Both B and D are wrong. Joining of cells is fertilisation.
B is wrong. Wind and some animals also carry pollen.

solution: A is correct: pollination is pollen landing on a stigma.
C is correct: the cells can join only after pollen has landed.
B is wrong (wind, water and animals carry pollen). D describes fertilisation.

questions.stem:
Which of the following statements about a flowering plant are correct?
A: The ovary grows into the fruit.
B: Pollen is made in the stigma.
C: Each fertilised ovule becomes a seed.
D: Petals grow into the seeds.

explain.why: D is wrong. Petals wither after pollination.
Both are wrong. The stigma receives pollen and petals wither.
B is wrong. Pollen is made in the anther.

solution: A and C are correct. B is wrong because pollen is made in the anther. D is wrong because petals do not become seeds.

questions.stem: Four flowers on a plant were treated as shown in the table. Insects visited all the flowers. Which flower is least able to make seeds?

explain.why: S has no sepals. The sepals do not take part in making seeds.
Q has no anthers, but it can still receive pollen carried from other flowers.
P has no petals, so fewer insects may visit, but its stigma can still receive pollen.

solution: Seeds form only if pollen lands on a stigma.
R has no stigma, so pollen cannot reach its ovules.

questions.stem: A farmer sprays a strong insecticide that kills all the bees in his orchard. Fewer fruits grow on his trees that season. What is the best reason?
options: The trees could not make any pollen without the bees
The petals fell off too soon for the fruits to grow
The roots took in less water from the soil that season
Less pollen reached the stigmas, so fewer flowers were fertilised

explain.why: The anthers of the trees make pollen on their own. Bees only carry it.
Petals falling off is normal after pollination. It does not reduce fruit by itself.
The insecticide killed bees. It was not about water in the roots.

solution: Bees carry pollen to stigmas.
With no bees, fewer stigmas get pollen, fewer ovules are fertilised and fewer fruits form.

questions.stem: Seedlings that grow right under their parent plant often grow poorly. What is the best reason?
options: They cannot be pollinated by insects or wind
They compete with the parent for light and water
They cannot make flowers or fruits
They have lost their seed coat too early

explain.why: Pollination happens in flowers, long before seedlings grow.
Seedlings are young. Flowers come later and are not the problem here.
A seed coat protects the seed. It has no effect on how the seedling grows later.

solution: Seedlings under the parent share the same light, water and soil.
That is why dispersing seeds far away helps new plants grow well.

questions.stem:
Which statements about spores and seeds are correct?
A: Both can grow into new plants.
B: A seed has stored food but a spore does not.
C: Spores are made in flowers.
D: Ferns make seeds inside fruits.

explain.why: C is wrong. Ferns and mosses have no flowers.
Both are wrong. Plants with spores have no flowers, fruits or seeds.
D is wrong. Ferns have no fruits or seeds.

solution: A and B are correct. C and D are wrong because spore plants have no flowers, fruits or seeds.

questions.stem: A gardener takes cuttings from a rose bush that has red flowers and plants them. What colour are the flowers of the new plants most likely to be?
options: Red, because they grow from a part of the parent plant
White, because cuttings are weaker than seeds
Pink, because the colour mixes with the soil
Any colour, because insects must pollinate the cuttings

explain.why: A cutting grows into a plant like its parent. Weakness does not change the colour.
Soil does not change the colour of the flowers.
Cuttings grow from stems. No pollination is involved.

solution: A cutting is a part of the parent plant, so the new plant is like the parent. Its flowers are red.

questions.stem: The picture shows a flower. Which row correctly gives the job of two of its labelled parts?
options: P: receives pollen; Q: makes pollen
P: attracts insects; Q: receives pollen
P: attracts insects; Q: grows into the fruit
P: makes pollen; Q: grows into the fruit

explain.why: Both are wrong: the petal does not receive pollen and the ovary does not make it.
Q is the ovary. The stigma (S) receives pollen.
P is a petal, which attracts insects. It does not make pollen.

solution: P is a petal and Q is the ovary. Petals attract insects, and the ovary grows into the fruit.

options: The petals are needed to carry pollen down to the ovary
The petals have done their job of attracting insects
The petals would stop the ovary from growing bigger
The petals have changed into the seeds of the fruit

explain.why: Petals do not carry pollen. Insects and wind do.
Petals do not affect the growth of the ovary.
The seeds come from the ovules, not the petals.

solution: Petals attract insects. Pollination has happened, so they are no longer needed.

The number of seeds put in each dish
The seeds that germinate in each dish
The colour of the dishes he uses

explain.why: The temperature must stay the same, so it is not what he measures.
This is the same (10) in all dishes. It is a variable kept the same.
The colour of the dish is not related to the question.

solution: The amount of water is the one thing changed.
The results to measure are how many seeds germinate in each dish.

The more water the seeds are given, the more seeds germinate
Seeds germinate best with some water, and too much lowers germination
Seeds that were given 5 mL of water germinated best

explain.why: With no water, none of the seeds germinated.
At 20 mL only 3 seeds germinated, fewer than at 10 mL.
Seeds given 10 mL did best (9 seeds), better than 5 mL (8 seeds).

solution: No water gave 0 seeds, 10 mL gave the most (9) and 20 mL gave only 3.
So some water is needed but too much is harmful.

questions.stem: A gardener grows a herb under a net that keeps out insects. He gently shakes the flowers every day and the plant makes fruits. How does shaking help?
options: The shaking makes the roots take in more water
The shaking joins the male and female cells directly
The shaking makes the petals grow into fruits
Pollen is shaken from the anthers onto the stigmas

explain.why: Shaking flowers does not change how roots take in water.
The cells join inside the ovule after pollen reaches the stigma. Shaking only helps pollination.
Fruits grow from the ovary, not the petals.

solution: Without insects, shaking moves pollen from the anthers to the stigmas, so pollination can happen.

questions.stem: Which of the following is evidence that a plant can reproduce without seeds?
options: A leaf placed on wet soil grows roots and a plant
A seed grows into a seedling in wet cotton wool
Bees visit the flowers of a plant
A fruit has many seeds inside it

explain.why: That is a seed growing, so it needs a seed.
Bees carrying pollen lead to seeds.
That shows seeds, not reproduction without them.

solution: A new plant that grows from a leaf grows from part of the parent plant. No seed is involved.

questions.stem: A coconut has a fibrous husk that holds air. Which of the following is the best reason why this helps the coconut palm reproduce?
options: The husk lets the wind lift it up like a wing
The coconut flower is pollinated by sea water
The husk stops the seed from ever germinating on land
The coconut floats and is carried by the sea to a new beach

explain.why: A coconut is heavy. It is carried by water, not the wind.
The husk is on the fruit, which forms after pollination.
The seed can germinate when it reaches a beach.

solution: Air in the husk makes the coconut float.
Sea water carries it to a new beach where it can germinate.

questions.stem: A student says: 'A flower with no ovary can never make a seed.' Which reason supports the student's statement?
options: Seeds grow from pollen, which is made in the ovary of a flower
Seeds grow from ovules, which are inside the ovary
The ovary attracts the insects that carry the pollen
The ovary is the part that receives the pollen

explain.why: Pollen is made in the anther, and seeds do not grow from pollen.
Petals attract insects, not the ovary.
The stigma receives pollen.

solution: An ovule becomes a seed after fertilisation. Ovules are inside the ovary.
Without an ovary there are no ovules.

questions.stem: Birds eat the berries of a plant. The seeds inside have a hard, smooth coat. Why is the hard coat useful to the plant?
options: It helps the seeds to stick to the bird's feathers and legs
It lets the seeds float on water
It makes the seeds light enough to be blown away by wind
It protects the inside from the bird's stomach juices

explain.why: A smooth coat does not stick. Hooks would do that.
These seeds are carried by birds, not by water.
A hard coat does not make a seed lighter. These seeds travel inside birds.

solution: The seeds pass through the bird's body and come out in the droppings.
The hard coat protects the inside of the seed from the juices that digest food.

questions.stem: Aisha wants to find out if seeds need air to germinate. Which two set-ups in the table should she compare?

explain.why: Q is dry and R is wet, so water is different too.
P and Q differ in water. They test water, not air.
P has cotton wool and S has tap water, so more than the air differs.

solution: R and S are both in water in a warm room. Only the air differs: R's water has no air (boiled and covered with oil).

questions.stem: Pollen from a rose flower lands on the stigma of a hibiscus flower. What is most likely to happen?
options: The rose flower makes seeds, because its pollen has been used
The pollen grows into a new rose plant on the hibiscus flower
The hibiscus flower does not make seeds, because the pollen cannot fertilise it
The hibiscus flower makes seeds, because pollen on any stigma fertilises it

explain.why: The rose flower is not involved here. Its own ovules were not fertilised.
Pollen does not grow into a plant. A seed forms only after fertilisation.
Pollen can only fertilise the ovules of a flower of the same kind of plant.

solution: Pollen from one kind of plant cannot fertilise the ovules of another kind, so fertilisation does not happen.
Without fertilisation, the hibiscus flower does not make seeds.

questions.stem: Aisha's results are in the table. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Seeds need both water and air to germinate
Seeds germinate best when covered with water
Seeds can germinate without water if there is air

explain.why: Light was not tested in any of the set-ups.
P (damp cotton wool) had more germinating seeds than S (in water).
Q had air but no water and no seeds germinated.

solution: Q (no water) shows that water is needed; R (no air) shows that air is needed.
P has both and nine seeds germinated.
